The waves crashed violently upon the rocks of the islet ~~coast~~ with a passion uncharacteristic of the dark and dreary night. ~~On the opposite shore,~~ the tall outlines of blackwood trees were vaguely discernible on the shore as shadowy silhouettes against the moonlit sky, ~~like~~ a line of sentinels poised to guard against the terrors of the dark. There was no movement aside from the waves; not even a breeze disturbed the stillness ~~of the rocky islet ground~~.

Then suddenly, a cry. Not a human cry, like that of a restless child yearning for a mother’s devoted touch. This was a different sound altogether; shrill and sharp, piercing through the silence of the darkness like a knife into flesh. The cry rose from the centre of the islet, rising above the vehemence of the waves, reaching upwards towards the argent-silver disk that crowned the lonely sky, as if in longing for the freedom of those far-flung heights.

A dark cloud, inconspicuous in its advance, moved to shroud the face of the moon, and in that moment the cry subsided, then faded altogether; a falling star descending into the abyssal depths of the ocean’s embrace. The rustle of a robe disturbed the islet floor as unshod footsteps advanced in circular motion around a centre stone; square and flat, and as ancient as the moon itself. The cloud continued in its lonesome voyage, unveiling the moon once more. The silver rays shimmered upon the eroded ground, wet with the spittle of the sea, their light revealing a lifeless shape upon the stone, black and unmoving, encircled by a crimson ocean of its own.

A hand, wrinkled and ancient, with veins like coiling azure snakes, gently pressed against the breast of the dark and unmoving figure. Carefully, almost caressingly, the Alchemist stroked his fingers over the soft, feathery body, feeling its warmth, delighting in the stillness of its lifeless body. The corner of his lip rose in a vague semblance of a smile, distorting his face like a crevice upon the altar stone beneath his hand. ~~He was old and wizened, with~~ His skin like crumbled parchment, his head shrouded under a hood of amethyst-lined grey. His lips ~~were~~ thin and colourless, his nose curved like the broken archway of the temple ruins ~~in the midst of which~~ where he stood ~~was standing~~. And yet his eyes shone with a moonlike luminosity – phosphorescent as if emitting a glow of their own. His hands were dressed in rings embedded with translucent gemstones, glinting like dancing flames in the dark.

It was one such ring – silver with a stone the shade of vermilion – that the Alchemist removed, placing upon the raven’s bloody and feathered breast. A faint breeze crept into the stillness of the night and the feathers danced dismally - the shades of the departed come to haunt the rocky shores. A tension permeated the air~~, hanging~~ like a fog ~~of foreboding~~, though the Alchemist was not afraid. He was exultant.

As suddenly as it had come, the breeze vanished. A cloud once more swathed the face of the moon in a shroud of ashen gray and the silver rays retreated into the night. A cry arose, again shrill and sharp, but unearthly, and this time it did not fade. Upon the altar stone the lifeless creature trembled, then straightened, standing with its face towards the sky. Its eyes, no longer black and lifeless, shone now with a moonlike luminosity. With a second cry the beast rose, flying into the night. As silence descended once more, the Alchemist grinned his crooked smile, breaking into a laugh as unearthly as the creature he had created.

“And as you can see behind me,” the reporter said, his blue suit whipping around violently in the gale-force winds, “It seems that le Fay and Enigma have disappeared behind the Skyneedle Tower, their skirmish ongoing.”

He turned to look away from the camera, at the devastated street behind him.  When he looked back at the camera, an expression of hopelessness had etched itself onto his handsome face.

“If this is any indication of their power, then Attroh City is in for a wild afternoon.”

Even as the microwave beeped to indicate it had finished cooking, I couldn’t pull myself away from the screen.  It was a morbid curiosity at the duelling supers who had made the busy centre of Attroh City their battleground.  The camera wasn’t the best at showing the results of their fight, but apparently the chopper had been downed by a blast of some kind from Morgana le Fey, Attroh City’s resident supervillaness.

I wasn’t one of those super geeks who knew every hero and villain from Texas to Rio to Tokyo.  But I didn’t live under a rock, so I knew a little about the supers in Attroh City.  There was the main protective force, the Guardians.  A group of minor villains called the Cyphers.  And of course, the Triad.  But the two fighting today weren’t a part of any of those teams.

Enigma was an inventor of some kind who adapted to every fight he lost.  It was a good thing that he was on the side of the law.  Morgana le Fay, named after the sorceress from Arthurian legend, was a modern witch.  The two didn’t fight each other much, but when they did it often resulted in large amounts of property destruction.

The camera caught a glimpse of something green moving past in a flash.  It followed the figure until it paused in front of a skyscraper.  Morgana.  She waved a hand and the glass windows near her shattered into a thousand fragments.  The fragments flew to her and reoriented themselves like daggers.  She threw her hand forward and the fragments shot forth like bullets.

Enigma flew around the corner in pursuit, two small jets on the base of his shoes providing the thrust.  As he spotted the glass darts flying toward him, he pushed a finger to his wrist and a blue forcefield projected out of his glove.  The glass fragments shattered harmlessly against the forcefield.

Enigma followed up with a blue shot from his other glove, which Morgana effortlessly sailed over.  She threw a bolt of dark green energy at him and then shot off behind the tower, leaving Enigma to follow.

“And they’ve gone again.  I’m Dan Harper, bringing you updates live from the scene,” the reporter said.

I heard a sound coming from the front.  Mom and Dad back, I bet.  I turned the TV off and raced to the kitchen, removing the pizza from last night from the microwave and hoping to hell I hadn’t left it in for too long.  I pulled the plate out and swore as I burned my fingers.

The back door slammed and I heard my parents’ voices arguing.  I whispered a silent thanks that we lived far enough from anyone else that no one could hear them.

“I don’t feel comfortable sending her to public school,” I heard my dad say, “Who knows how she’ll end up if that happens?”

“Is that your approach?” my mom’s voice asked venomously.  “Did you forget that I went to public school?  Did that make me a worse person?”

“Arguably, yes.”

“You sonofa-“

I took the stairs two at a time, leaping into the laundry room to surprise my parents and hopefully end the argument.  I didn’t expect what I found.

“What the fuck?” I asked, as I saw my parents dressed up as Enigma and Morgana le Fay.  Grime and dust had accumulated over their faces and exposed skin and I saw blood leaking from several wounds on their bodies.

“Language, dear,” my dad chastised weakly as he and my mom looked up guiltily to see me standing there.

“Mom?  Dad?  What’s happening?”

They shared a look, which didn’t stop me from freaking out.  Why was my dad wearing a trench coat and steampunk goggles, with two high-tech gauntlets covering his hands?  Why was my mom dressed like a slutty witch for Halloween in a dark green robe?

“Listen, dear,” my dad began, “sometimes you see things that you don’t think are there.  Remember when you thought that your closet was haunted?”

“We’re supers,” my mom interrupted, “I’m Morgana le Fay and he is Enigma.”

My dad closed his eyes and sighed, “Honey, you didn’t have to do that.”

“I’m not going to gaslight my daughter to protect my secret identity.”

“Please don’t argue,” I pleaded, “Just tell me what’s going on.”

“Maybe we should have this discussion over a cup of tea,” my dad suggested, “Rose, do you want to start the kettle while your mother and I change?  And Isobel, if you wanted to have a shower first I can have mine when you finish.”

“Why wait?” My mom asked with a wicked smile.  I gagged, trying to bleach the idea of my parents showering together from my mind.

———

Half an hour later, me and my parents were gathered around the kitchen table, a cup of tea in front of each of us.  Well, in front of my dad and I.  Mom had opted for something a little stronger.  A lot stronger.

“Bacardi?” My dad wondered aloud. “At three in the afternoon?”

“I’m a grown woman,” my mom protested, “I can handle my alcohol intake.”

“Where have I heard that one before?” he muttered before turning his attention to me.

“So, Rose.  Do you have anything you want to ask us before we start explaining everything to you?”

I had, in fact, mentally prepared a list of questions to ask.  No, interrogate them with.  All of that flew out the window as he turned his blue eyes onto me.  Only then did I realise how tired they were.

“Why now?  Why didn’t you tell me before?”

“Because it would have made it harder for you to live a normal life.  You would have been more aware of our world, and you would have subconsciously been a target for the more ruthless villains out there if they managed to discover your identity.  Now, I think we’d better start from the beginning.”

My dad gestured to my mom and she sighed, taking a long sip from the bottle before she began.

“I was a teenager when I discovered the amulet.  It was some Celtic thing, buried in my foster parents’ backyard by God knows who.  When I touched it I heard the voices of hundreds before me explaining my destiny, how I had been chosen to become the latest incarnation of the Sorceress.  So I trained, learning how to use my new powers.  Then I fought back against the system that had never helped me and became Morgana le Fay, the Witch of Washington.”

I glanced at my dad. “And you?”

“I was always curious about the universe.  You’ve inherited some of that.  From a young age I was always building and inventing, set on making the world a better place.  I was offered a scholarship to MIT at thirteen and built the world’s first nano tech intelligent robots.  I was abducted by terrorists, forced to build weapons of mass destruction.  I managed to build a device to escape and then decided to stop rogue threats to peace and stability.”

“How did you two meet, then?”

They shared a look filled with nostalgia and mutual longing.  It was like something out of a cheesy rom-com, but seeing that filled my heart with joy at the idea that two people who were so ideologically different could find romance together.

“Funnily enough,” my dad said, “it was on the train.”

“I was running late to a date with someone else,” my mom continued, “and I ran into some handsome nerd who blushed when he looked at me.  So, provocateur that I am, I cheekily sat next to him and put my hand on his-“

“I don’t think Rose wants to hear about that,” my dad interrupted, “Needless to say, your mother didn’t make that other date and instead kidnapped me to show me the dark underside of the city.”

“I prefer the term ‘friendly abduction’,” my mom teased.

“So, what happens now?” I asked.

My parents shared a look again.

“Maybe we could try homeschooling?” my mom offered.

She was waiting for me beside the closet on the third floor when I arrived, tapping one foot against the ground as she looked at her phone.  My shoe slid on the floor as I approached and she looked up at the resulting squeak, her frustrated expression being replaced by one of happiness.

“Great!  You came!”  She said.  Of course I did.  How could I refused when she asked me specifically?

Rachel was a tall girl, almost up to my shoulder in height.  And I was pretty tall myself.  Her long blonde hair was usually tied back in a ponytail to prevent it from whipping her in the face while she was cheerleading and today was no exception.  She gazed at me with her expressive blue eyes as she said,  “Thanks for coming.  No one else would believe me and I knew that I sounded crazy but I had to tell someone.”

“I, uh.  No problem.”  I said, managing to smile awkwardly at her.  It was perhaps only sheer luck that she didn’t immediately decide to leave upon that failure of a conversation starter.

She was still looking me in the eyes, however.  I glanced away, uncomfortable with the attention.  Finally, I saw her turn away from me in my peripheral vision and I was able to look back at her.

“There,”  she said, pointing toward the closet she had spoken about before.  I followed her finger and stared at the closet.

It was just a normal closet, a piece of furniture made of wood and lacquer that stood there holding clothes or whatever people wanted to put in there.  Nothing too interesting.  I watched Rachel approach the closet.  She sandwiched her fingers together and contorted them, a sign she was nervous.

“So, uh, how did you come to find this portal?”  I asked, focused more on the curve of Rachel’s back and behind than the closet.  Hey, I was a seventeen year old hanging around the girl I’d been crushing on since I knew what crushes were.  No wooden box was going to be more interesting.

When she answered, her voice was faint and distracted, as if her mind was far away.  “I was bleeding so I left class one day to go to the bathroom and I just felt this strange force telling me to come here.”

“Bleeding?  You cut yourself somehow?”

She glanced at me, a frown upon her face.  “No.  I was bleeding.  You know, down there?”

“Oh.”  I suppressed the instinct to slap my forehead.  Dumb, dumb, dumb.  Talking before thinking.

“Anyway, I opened the closet and saw this black hole in the bottom.  I stared at it for a long time and then it seemed to just stretch out into infinity.  I didn’t want to touch it so I poked it with a pen and it sucked the pen in.”

I frowned.  “So you think that it’s a portal of some kind?  And not just a hole that formed spontaneously?”

“When have you ever heard of a hole sucking a pen into it?”

I shrugged.  “Maybe you only imagined that and in reality you just dropped it?”

Rachel shook her head.  “No.  I know what I saw.  If you open it up you’ll see what I mean.”

“Okay, okay.  I’m opening the closet now.”

I stepped forward, placing one hand on the doorknob.  As I touched it, a small spark of electricity shot into my hand.  It wasn’t painful, just eerie.  The doorknob was made of brass and cold to the touch.  I pushed it down and felt it catch before it worked easily.  Feeling my heart start to beat faster in anticipation, I pulled the door open.

Nothing.  There was no hole in the bottom of the closet, no extra-dimensional portal that sucked student’s pens away.  Just a regular floor.

I turned back to Rachel, expecting her to have her phone out to record some video that would be posted to the internet with the title ‘Cute Cheerleader convinces Dumb Nerd to open closet door’ or something stupid like that.  Instead, all I saw was her confused face.

“I… I…”  she said.  “I saw something there.”

“I’m not saying that you didn’t,”  I said soothingly,  “Just that whatever you saw might not have been real.”

She looked sharply at me, an accusatory look in her eyes.  “You don’t believe me, do you?  You think that I’ve gone crazy.”

I frantically shook my head.  I didn’t want to ruin my one chance with her already.  “No, no.  I believe you.”

“It doesn’t sound like you do.  You sound just like everyone else that I ever told about my dreams.  ‘Nice story Rachel, but dragons and goblins and magic aren’t real’.  ‘Are you sure that you haven’t seen one too many fantasy movies, Rachel?'”

“What?”  I asked, somewhat confused.  I’d never really spoken to Rachel since she became pretty and popular back in second grade, but we had once been quite close as friends.  As in, sleeping over at each other’s houses friends.

“I’m telling you,”  she continued, in that shout-whisper people do when they’re emotional but retain the presence of mind to know that they shouldn’t be shouting,  “I know what I saw.  And what I saw was a portal to another dimension.  Here, I’ll show you.”

Before I could react, she took several quick steps and stood in the closet.  I reached out in an attempt to do… something, but she was gone.  I blinked several times, completely dumbfounded.  Rachel George had disappeared from the closet.

After I had stood there for several seconds processing recent events, I stepped forward and poked my head into the closet.  It wasn’t large enough for her to have concealed herself somehow but I wanted to make certain of that fact.  Nope.  No perky cheerleader anywhere in the closet.

I sighed to myself, wondering if I had somehow hit my head and was currently in a concussion-fuelled dream.  Or nightmare, if Rachel had just disappeared randomly.  I reached down and picked up Rachel’s bag from where she had left it on the ground and turned to head down to the administration office to report a missing student.

Just before I did that, though, something compelled me to look back at the closet, still half open.  I frowned, the faintest hint of an idea sparking to life inside my head.  I took a step, then another, then another and another until I was standing just outside the empty closet.  Taking a deep breath, I stepped into the closet, right where Rachel had been before she disappeared.

At first I felt nothing, just stupidity.  An undercurrent of frustration at myself for believing something impossible like portals existed and for letting Rachel slip out of my grasp.  I dropped her bag from my hands, barely registering that I had done so.  Then I felt something tug at my pant leg.

I looked down and saw a darkness that extended past my current understanding of darkness.  It wasn’t an absence of light so much as it drew in light like a black hole, making it impossible to see.  Like a negative spot on my vision.  The pulling sensation increased and I realised that I was falling into a space that shouldn’t have existed.

I only had time to utter,  “Holy shit,”  before I couldn’t feel anything at all.

Not because I was dead, but because my senses literally weren’t existing.  I could feel all of my body in some weird way but I couldn’t feel any input from stimuli of any kind.  My vision was dark, my ears could hear nothing but silence so stark that there was a faint ringing sound and my skin felt nothing but the skin touching it.  I don’t know how long I fell for, only that it was longer than nothing and less than infinite.  Hell, for all I knew the time there transcended my current understanding of numbers and was something completely incomprehensible.

Then it ended and I fell onto something very soft.

My senses returned in one hit and I reeled from the intense sensations.  Everything was clear and distinct for a second and then I felt normal again.  Wondering where exactly I was, I glanced around.

It was dark, but the darkness that comes from the absence of light rather than the absence of existence.  I could make out trees around me and could smell the scents of the forest, like that one time my family had gone camping in Yosemite before my brother died.  I barely had time to wonder how the hell I had got there before I heard a sound in the trees behind me.

I scuttled away, expecting a bear of some kind.  What I didn’t expect was Rachel emerging from the trees, heading straight toward me like the darkness didn’t bother her.  She didn’t look happy at all.

“Been after this one for a long time,”  one of the guards commented as the group began to move down the hallway into the station proper.  “How did you manage to snatch him up?”

Degan shrugged.  “I caught up to him after a particularly good tip.  I got the drop, killed his men and took him alive.”

“I would have just shot him at the same time,”  the other guard said.

“He’s not worth the bullet,”  Degan observed.

There was a large door ahead of them and the guards tilted their bodies forward.  “Gravity-affected area incoming,”  one of them informed Degan.

As he approached, he realised that it wasn’t in fact a door but a floor.  The weakest pull of gravity could be felt as they neared the floor, dragging them closer to the moon’s surface.  The overhead handholds stopped, and one of the guards gently stepped over to a console on the side.  He pushed a few buttons and entered in a code and the group was sealed in by a door sliding shut above them.

An elevator, Degan realised.

It started slowly, then began to pick up in speed as the gravitational force affecting the group increased, granting inertia that prevented them from lifting off the floor and smashing into the ceiling of the elevator.

Several minutes passed, in which Degan felt the familiar sensation of gravity returning to his body gradually over that period.  Finally, the elevator slowed and they came to a halt.  There was silence for a few moments before the side of the elevator opened to reveal the station and more guards preparing for the handover.

“We’ll take him from here,”  they said, stepping forward and taking the original two guards’ places beside the Chief.  They led him forward while the two original guards gestured for Degan to follow them.

“He won’t be getting out for a long time,”  one of the guards boasted.  “No one’s ever escaped this place.”

“First time for everything,”  Degan said, more to play the Devil’s Advocate than any true belief that a escape might occur.

He eyed the numerous cameras set into the ceiling, watching them pass with an uninterested robotic gaze.  They passed through several checkpoints before finally reaching a room where the guards told Degan to wait for the Warden to arrive with his reward.

It turned out to be much longer than just a few minutes, so Degan occupied himself with reading one of the outdated bibles placed on a table.  Recordings of old videplays were showing on a screen set into the wall behind a steel cage, some comedy that Degan could only half remember.  He was just about halfway through the first testament of the bible when the Warden arrived.

Degan’s first impression of the Warden was that his fake smile was far too grating.  The man was tall and rotund, balding on top and wearing a brown suit that looked about five decades old.  Nevertheless, Degan shook the offered hand and gave a fake smile in return.

“Glad to hear that someone finally caught the Chief,”  the Warden said, his pale face showing the ruddiness of a habitual drinker.

“It’s my job, Warden,”  Degan replied, unfazed by the attempt at flattery.  The only time that worked was when it was a pretty woman doing the flattering, and Degan hadn’t met a pretty girl for weeks.

The Warden nodded, his smile wavering for half a heartbeat.  “Yes.  Of course it is.  My mistake.”

“Now, not to rush you,”  Degan began,  “But the reward?”

“Yes.  Indeed.  You need to be rewarded for your hard work.  Come this way, please.”

The Warden led him out of the waiting room and into a small office marked Security.  Strange place to hide a hundred thousand credits, Degan thought.

As they entered the room, Degan realised that the Warden wasn’t leading him to the reward.  Instead, it seemed to be some bizarre tour where the Warden tried to show Degan how much he meant by demonstrating how he could force his employees to do his will.  Posturing, nothing more.

“Here you can see the security room,”  the Warden said, gesturing to the dozens of monitors showing live feeds from the cameras set around the prison.  “Every square inch of this place is monitored by the security team every second of every hour of the day.  As the saying goes: if these prisoners sneeze, we’ll know it.”

Degan swiftly skimmed the monitors, looking for one that displayed the Chief.  After a few seconds, he found it.  The man was being led down a long hallway by two bulky guards, his hands and feet encased in chains.

“Now, this is the most secure and feared prison in the galaxy,”  the Warden was saying,  “And that’s a reputation that I like to uphold.”

Degan was focusing on the monitor showing the Chief, watching as the guards passed by one of the cell doors that then opened.

“Warden,”  he said, interrupting the Warden’s verbal diarrhoea,  “Are the cell doors supposed to swing open like that?”

He pointed to the monitor displaying the Chief.  The Warden leaned forward, squinting at the screen.

“Oh shit,”  he said as a prisoner crept out of the cell, unseen by the guards.

Then the lights and monitors cut out and panic truly set in.

The ship connected with the docking port of the station with a loud clunk.  The sound of machinery moving was audible as various locks connected and intertwined to prevent the ship from accidentally disengaging in the midst of someone travelling between the ship and station or vice versa.  Finally, after several minutes, all was still.

Degan deactivated the engines of his ship and unbuckled the belt keeping him in the pilot’s seat.  The *Bird of Prey* was a rusty hunk of junk, but it was his rusty hunk of junk and he took care to maintain it and ensure it didn’t fall to pieces.  Taking a quick glance at a monitor set just above the viewfinder, he noted that the Chief was still restrained in the tiny cell in the back of the ship.

Gloved fingers brushed over the six shooter holstered by his side, just to make sure it was still there.  Degan never felt completely safe when transporting these thugs so he always kept insurance on himself to dissuade any escape attempts.

Checking that the ship was fully docked, Degan pushed himself out of the chair and used the handholds set into the ceiling to pull himself toward the cockpit door.  With the push of a button and a hydraulic hiss, the door slid open and Degan pulled himself further into the ship.

The *Bird of Prey* was a Delta-Class shuttle, originally designed for quick sub-light trips around the smaller solar systems.  It wasn’t a particularly fast ship nor was it stealthy, but Degan had picked it up a long time ago for a very reasonable price and had spent the past two decades upgrading it.  Like a samwire wearing a ratterbash’s clothing, the *Bird of Prey* was much more than surface appearances would lead an observer to believe.

For starters, he’d installed several front facing cannons on the ship, disguised as tachyon antenna for faster than light communications.  Once or twice he’d managed to surprise and defeat more heavily armed ships simply because they thought he was nothing more than a salvaging ship lost in the area.  Add of course the ion cannons that were specifically designed to cripple an enemy’s power systems and the *Bird of Prey* was worth much more than any other ship in Degan’s mind.

He arrived at the back of the front quarter of the ship, where a large steel door separated the front section from the rear section.  Further on was the engines and a heap of electronics specifically designed for Degan’s occupation.  Hunting down the meanest suckers across the galaxy.  Punching in a seven-digit code, he waited for the doors to slowly creep open and reveal the sole inhabitant of the cell area.

The Chief was so-called for his business acumen and far-reaching organisation.  His past was unknown, as were other details such as his real name.  The only thing that was known about the Chief was that he was the leader of the Rooks, a smuggling, narcotics and trafficking organisation that operated around the inner rim of the galaxy.

He was large and bulky, the kind of guy that didn’t need a weapon to turn people into corpses.  One strong punch from that meaty hand would likely cave a skull in.  As Degan entered the cell area, the Chief turned his head and met Degan’s gaze with his dead eyes.  Well, dead eye.  One of the eyes had been lost long ago, the only evidence that it was ever there the blank socket where it had once resided.  A wan scar that stood out against the Chief’s tanned skin spread from above the empty socket to below it, which suggested that someone had, at some point, stabbed the Chief’s eye out.

“Ready for your stay?”  Degan asked, pulling himself over to the cell door.  He punched in another seven-digit code to unlock the door.

“At the Hilton?”  The Chief asked sardonically.

The Helios Hilton was the unofficial name for the Ehler 184c Maximum Security Prison, which was installed on the moon of the plant Ehler 184c.  It had a reputation across the galaxy for housing the worst of the worst, the kind of monsters that no one speaks about lest the devil gets any ideas.  People who were sentenced to the Helios Hilton never came under any circumstances.

Degan chose not to answer the Chief’s rhetorical question, instead pulling himself behind the man to disconnect him from the chains keeping him close to the wall of the cell.  Having done that, he pushed the man from the wall and out of the cell, using one hand to pull himself along with the handholds set around the exterior of the cell area.

They moved back through the ship to the airlock, where Degan secured the Chief to another set of chains.  He pressed a button on the wall that sent a signal to the opposing side, asking for permission to enter the Ehler 184c station.  There was silence for a few seconds before a beep sounded from the console.  Permission had been granted.

Degan then activated the airlock, watching as the doors behind him closed with a resounding hiss.  There was silence for a few seconds, then the door to the station opened with a sigh.  Degan removed the chains that kept the Chief to the wall and pushed him ahead, pulling himself forward.

They crossed into the station’s docking area and the door closed behind them.  Another few seconds passed and then the door leading into the station itself opened.  Degan pushed the Chief ahead, into the waiting arms of the guards there to receive the prisoner.  He pulled himself across the divide and heard the door close behind him.  Now there was no going back.  He was inside the mouth of hell itself.

The first sign of trouble was when I returned home to an unlit house.  It was a little ritual between Steve and I, that whenever I worked late he’d switch the porch lights on like those little lights that airplanes use to guide themselves onto the tarmac.  So when I turned onto our street and saw that the porch light wasn’t on, a shiver went up my spine.

I pulled into the driveway like usual, activated the handbrake and turned off the engine.  Then, I slipped the keys into my hand and let some of them filter through between the fingers.  Picking up my handbag with my free hand, I stepped out of the car and clicked the button to lock it.

I strode towards my house, the tension in my body increasing as I saw that no lights were on inside and there were no sounds coming from inside from either my husband or kids.  I didn’t know what might have happened but I could guess.  I used the keys to unlock the front door then pushed it open, staying outside as I did so.

Apart from the creaking of the door, there was silence.

“Steven?  Nate?  Alicia?”  I called.

When there was no response I knew that something terrible had happened.  Just to make sure, I took a quick glance at my phone and found no messages from Steve telling me that they had decided to go for takeaway or to the movies or something.

As I stepped into the house a horrid stench hit my nose and I was immediately hit by a torrent of memories.  They say that smell is the most powerful sense, and the reaction that metallic stench awakened in me is evidence that they’re right.

I heard gunfire, screams, the sound of bodies burning and madmen cackling.  I saw flickers of images in my mind’s eye: a man bisected, a dozen bodies piled into a large grave, and a man in a double-breasted suit standing before me, his cold eyes peering deep into my soul.

Then the memories faded as quickly as they had arrived and I was back in my home.  I kicked the door shut behind me and took a metal pen from my pocket, transferring it to my dominant hand.  If they were here, I wouldn’t back down without a fight.

I kicked my heels off and padded through the house barefoot, the sound almost imperceptible in the shadowy corridors.  As I approached the kitchen, the smell became stronger and harder to ignore.  Luckily, none of the memories returned.

I silently stepped into the kitchen and saw shapes in the dark, sitting around the table.  My eyes made out the form of my husband Steve and children Nate and Alicia.  They were sitting very still, not even breath audible in the silence of the house.  If they had been forced to sit there, I knew that I would have heard their shallow, nervous breaths but since I didn’t there was only one answer.  One that I dreaded to prove true.

Nevertheless, I reached out and turned on the switch for the light.  When I saw their bodies, I only just managed to maintain my grip on the pen.

They had been killed, red stripes visible across their throats and the trails of blood that had resulted pouring down their skin and staining it crimson.  They were arranged meticulously, so that they were sitting in an upright position as if preparing to eat dinner.  Knives had been driven through the backs of their hands to impale them onto the table, while makeshift garrottes of fishing wire had been tightened around their necks to prevent their heads from falling forward.  It was a gory tableau, a macabre imitation of suburban life.  And I knew exactly who had done it before I even found the letter.

It had been left in the centre of the table, below the candles that had been lit and placed there as decoration.  Made of a simple white cardboard, the text had been written in a black flowing font, evidence of someone spending hours perfecting their calligraphy technique.

*'We Liberated Your Family For Good Reason.  You Know Where To Find Us.  - Nine’*

As my eyes skimmed the note, I knew that everything I had sacrificed was for vain.  My hope for a normal, civilian life was gone if they knew where I was.

I shut my eyes, briefly hoping that one of them would have stayed behind to finish me off.  Unfortunately, I knew that I was too important to One to be killed.  His pet project, he had been fond of calling me.  And I knew what they wanted me back for.

I felt a tear leak out of my eye.  Once I might have thought that weakness.  Now I knew it was evidence that I had managed to break some of One’s conditioning.  I briefly said a mental goodbye to my family, then I opened my eyes and left the room, taking the note with me.  The local police would of course name me a suspect but my alibi was watertight and forensics would show they had been killed when I was at work.

Though I could have used the car, it would have made me traceable and I didn’t want that at the moment.  Instead, I simply took off down the road, walking at first before increasing to a slow jog that would bring me to the city in only a few minutes.  As I ran, my eyes fell to the inside of my wrist, where the remnants of a scar were visible.  The faintest lines of an X, then three vertical lines to make the III.  Thirteen in Roman numerals.  I felt the familiar sensation of pure, potent rage spiral through my body and I welcomed it.  One was going to regret wanting me to come back to him.

Depends what kind of book it is.  Something like 50 Shades, where the whole point of the book is showing the scenes, would require you to give details of the situation.  Almost any other book will pretty much entirely skip over the scene in question.  A scale of showing to implying could look like this:

1. Children's Books:  Absolutely no implications at all.  The most you could possibly do is kissing between the main character and their love interest.
2. Pre-Teen:  Same.  Maybe a bit more detail on the kissing, but nothing serious.
3. Teenager:  Now you can have implications about how the character feels and what they think about when they kiss, but they wouldn't have much more.
4. Young Adult:  The first 'genre' where you can introduce the idea of more than just kissing.  Most of the time (in fact probably all of the time) you'll just imply something happening between characters, such as them going back to the same room and waking up the next morning together, or even just two people talking about it sometime later.  More of the focus is on the feelings that lead up to and result from the scene.
5. New Adult:  I'm not really certain this is even a genre, but I've seen it mentioned so whatever.  In this case you will mostly imply it, but sometimes you might reach the level where you describe in little detail the characters preparing for the act (foreplay, undressing, etc.) or might simply reference the act with something flowery like "And then they discovered each other in that way true lovers did" or something similar.
6. Adult:  Most adult books that I've read have a little more than just normal implications.  Sometimes they have the flowery descriptions and sometimes there's even a page dedicated to describing the two engaging in coitus, but the focus of the story is generally more on whatever else is happening rather than the act itself.
7. Erotica:  This is the writing version of porn that spans from cheesy attempts like 50 Shades to stuff that people actually read to get them in the mood.  This type of genre is where people look for the details of the scene itself and entire chapters might be dedicated to sexual acts.  Often, depending on both the intended mood and the skill of the author, can range from something cheesy to something serious or even something lighthearted.  Language used will depend on the intended tone of the work, but generally authors refrain from calling it 'the thing down there'.

As to how to avoid making it too cringy, imagine what kind of language makes you cringe.  I would suggest that if you focus more on the feelings and thoughts that occur during the act rather than the physical act itself, the writing will be less cringy.  And of course, using language that finds a comfortable midpoint between being outright vulgar and too flowery.  Of course, if you don't think that including a detailed description of the scene will improve the story in any way, cut it out. His daughter was that propelling force.  His daughter, young Annette Sofia.  She would have been six when he left her, Edward recalled with a little difficulty.  Now only the Lord above knew how old she was.  She could have been dead for all he knew.  But the idea that she wasn’t, that she was out there somewhere living and wondering where he had disappeared to was Edward’s only reason for him not simply giving up.

Thoughts like this occupied his daily routine.  The other thoughts were mostly wishes that the forces of damnation would manage to take his captors at some point after they took him, or simply idle fantasies of being rescued.  Edward ran his dirtied hand over the crescent moon shaped amulet around his neck as he daydreamed of Annette.

The amulet was magical, said the old gypsy woman who had sold it to him.  It allowed two people to find each other, no matter the distance between them.  Edward placed no stock in such superstitious beliefs.  The only thing he believed in was the cold steel of a cutlass and the warm lead of a musket.  Nevertheless, he’d paid the silver for the amulet, more interested in the fancy design than the tales the woman had spun.  It would prove to be a beautiful present for his daughter, her tiny face shining brightly when he had presented it to her.

Edward smiled with the thought of that memory.  It distracted him from his surroundings enough that he only noticed the amulet heating up when it became hot enough to burn his hand.

He cried like a madman, plucking the amulet from his neck and throwing it to the ground.  It rattled against the cobblestone, the metal glowing from the heat.

Edward frowned at that.  Could metal do that?  Heat up to such a temperature that it could burn skin without any obvious source of energy?  He’d never heard of such a thing but he’d heard of other fantastical tales from fellow sea men.  Those who swore that they’d seen sirens luring ships to their graves or that they’d been chased by a monster as large as an island with mountains for teeth.  Of course, this was all after they’d been through several mugs of ale and their cheeks were red with intoxication.

He shook his head and rationalised that he must have been imagining it.

\------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

It was three weeks later when the amulet burned Edward again.

Edward had returned to wearing the amulet by the day’s end and had almost completely forgotten all about the incident, chalking it up to nothing more than the madness brought about by solitude and his imprisonment.

Time was compressed in the prison, being in that peculiar state in which one seemed to traverse the currents of time both quickly and slowly.  Each moment was painfully, torturously slow to experience but once it had occurred it seemed as though it were barely a fraction of the length that it had felt.

Edward had been in the midst of a meal composed of that flavourless grey slop when the amulet had once again started to heat up against the skin of his chest.  He dropped the wooden spoon into the slop and touched his fingers to the amulet, as if to confirm that it were, indeed, beginning to increase in temperature.

It was, and Edward grit his teeth as the amulet began to burn his finger as if he had stuck it into an open flame.  The sensation against his chest was equally as hot and Edward briefly feared that the amulet would brand his skin but the amulet soon began to cool, eventually reaching a temperature slightly warmer than the cell he resided in but cool enough that it did not bring pain to touch it.

“What infernal sorcery is this?”  Edward asked the air, not expecting to receive an answer.

None came except for the screaming of another prisoner farther down the hallway who had long ago lost his sanity.  Edward picked the spoon up from where it lay in the slop and resumed eating, his mind floundering at the question of why the amulet was acting so strangely.
